summary: A table of commonly seen header fields in email message headings. It is informational and serves as a handy reference for what these headers are used for.

plainLanguage.summary: Every email starts with a block of header fields, each one a line or two saying who it is from, who it is for and what it is about. Those fields are defined in many different documents. This memo gathers them into one table and explains each one.

questions: what do email header fields mean
what does the reply-to header do
subtitle: One table of the header fields that turn up at the top of email and news messages, and what each one means.

tldr.problem: The header fields of a mail message are defined across many different RFCs, so nobody has the whole picture in one place.
tldr.mechanism: The memo collects the headers found in ten Internet standards and in common use, gives each a short description, marks each with the RFC that defines it and with a warning where the header is unusual.
tldr.outcome: The result is a reference table for anyone building a mail system, with two appendices: one listing the headers by the RFC they come from and one in alphabetical order.

today: RFC 2076 is an Informational memo from February 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a reference table, and the author said at the time that he intended to keep updating it, with a later version available for download from his own web site.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Many different Internet standards and RFCs define headers which may occur on Internet mail messages and on Usenet news articles. The intention of this document is to list all such headers in one document as an aid to people developing message systems or interested in Internet mail standards. For each header the memo gives a short description and a reference to the Internet standard or RFC in which the header is defined.

The tables cover the headers the author found in RFC 822, RFC 1036, RFC 1123, RFC 1327, RFC 1496, RFC 1521, RFC 1766, RFC 1806, RFC 1864 and RFC 1911, plus a few headers that often turn up in mail but are not part of any Internet standard. Some things are deliberately left out. The heading attributes defined in PEM and MOSS are not included, because those headers appear inside the body of a message and so are not headers in the RFC 822 sense. Mail attributes in envelopes, that is the attributes controlling the message transport mechanism between mail and news servers, are not included either, which means that attributes from SMTP, UUCP and NNTP are mainly not covered. Headings used only in HTTP are not included yet, but may be included in a future version of the memo.

The memo also fixes the vocabulary. A heading is formatted text at the top of a message, ended by a blank line. A header, also called a heading field, is one field in the heading, beginning with a field name, a colon, and followed by the field values. Header names are spelled the way they are actually used, which is usually American but sometimes English spelling, and the header Organisation/Organization appears with either spelling.
sections.plainLanguage: A header field is one name and value pair, such as Subject followed by a colon and the subject line. The memo is careful about which headers count, and about how each one is spelled in practice.

sections.title: How to Read the Table
sections.content:
Two kinds of marker are used in the tables. Headers that RFC 1327 defines for use in messages from or to Internet mail and X.400 gateways are marked not for general usage, because they have not been standardized for general use between Internet mail-based systems. Headers defined only in RFC 1036 for Usenet news are marked not standardized for use in e-mail, because they have no standard meaning there and some of them may even be used in different ways by different software. RFC 1036, although generally used as a de-facto standard for Usenet news, is not an official IETF standard or even on the IETF standards track.

The other markers describe the state of a header. Non-standard means the header is not specified in any of the referenced RFCs, and appears in the table only because it often turns up in mail or news; using it is not generally recommended. Discouraged means the header is non-standard, is known to create problems and should not be generated, and handling it in incoming mail should be done with great caution. Controversial means the meaning and usage of the header is controversial, because different implementors have chosen to implement it in different ways, so it should be handled with caution and understanding of the different possible interpretations. Experimental means the header is newly defined and is to be tried out before entering the IETF standards track, and should only be used if both communicating parties agree to use it.

The memo adds one more caution of its own. RFC 1327 defines headers that map X.400 attributes which were previously not standardized in Internet mail, so the fact that a header occurs in RFC 1327 indicates that it is recommended for gatewaying messages between X.400 and Internet mail, but does not mean that the header is recommended for messages wholly within Internet mail. Some of these headers may eventually see widespread implementation and use in Internet mail, but at the time of writing, in 1996, they are not widely implemented or used. Headers defined only in RFC 1036 for Usenet news sometimes appear in mail messages, either because the messages were gatewayed from news to e-mail or because they were written in combined clients, and they are not standardized for use in Internet e-mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry in the table carries a warning label. Some headers are for one kind of network only, some are not standard at all, and some are so open to interpretation that a program should be careful with them.

sections.title: Who the Message Is From and Who It Is For
sections.content:
The largest group of headers covers who a message is from and who it is for. From names the authors or the people taking responsibility for the message. Sender names the person or agent submitting the message to the network, if that is different from the From header. To lists the primary recipients, cc the secondary and informational recipients, and bcc the recipients not to be disclosed to the other recipients.

The memo warns about two headers that look similar but are not the same. The header From, with a space instead of a colon, is used in the Unix mailbox format, also known as the Berkeley mailbox format or the MBOX format, where a line beginning with From separates successive messages in a file. It appears when a text editor looks at a file in that format, and some mailers use it when printing messages on paper. The information in it should not be used to find an address to which replies are to be sent. A third variant, From with a greater-than sign in front of it, is used in Usenet news mail transport to indicate the path an article took when transferred to a new host, and is sometimes called the From_ header.

Response control is the next group. Reply-To indicates where the sender wants replies to go, but the memo calls it ambiguous, because there are different kinds of replies and the sender may want them to go to different addresses: personal replies intended for one person, and group replies intended for the whole group of people who read the replied-to message, which is often a mailing list. Some mail systems use Reply-To to give a better form of the sender's address, and some mailing list expanders put the name of the list in it; both practices are controversial, and the author's personal opinion is that the header should be avoided except in special cases. Followup-To, defined for Usenet news, says where future discussion of an article should go, and its value must always be one or more newsgroup names, never e-mail addresses. Disclose-Recipients says whether recipients are to be told the names of the other recipients. Alternate-Recipient controls whether a message may be forwarded to alternate recipients such as a postmaster if delivery to the intended recipient is not possible, and the default is Allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: The address headers are the ones most mail programs touch. The memo's warning is about the three different ways the word From can be written, only one of which is an address.

sections.title: Identifying a Message and Pointing at Others
sections.content:
Message-ID is the unique ID of the message, and Content-ID the unique ID of one body part of the message content. In-Reply-To references the message this message is a reply to, and References refers to other related messages in e-mail, or to replied-to articles in Usenet news. See-Also, Supersedes, Article-Updates and Article-Names are Usenet headers, the last two only in Usenet news, and all are marked non-standard. Obsoletes refers to a previous message being corrected and replaced, and the memo notes that this field may in the future be replaced with Supersedes.

The difference between Obsoletes and Supersedes matters. In Usenet news, Supersedes causes a full deletion of the replaced article in the server, while in e-mail the behaviour is implemented in the client and often does not remove the old version of the text. Article-Updates is similar to Supersedes but does not cause the referenced article to be physically deleted, and Article-Names is for reference to particularly important articles in a given newsgroup.

Other textual headers carry free text. Subject is the title or heading and is often used as a thread indicator for messages that reply to or comment on other messages. Keywords are search keys for database retrieval, and Comments are comments on a message. Content-Description describes a particular body part of a message. Summary is a short text describing a longer article, and the memo warns that some mail systems will not display this text to the recipient, so it should not be used for text the recipient must be sure of getting. Organization names the organization the sender of an article belongs to, and the Organisation spelling is non-standard.
sections.plainLanguage: These headers let one message point at another, so that a mail program can gather a conversation together. Message-ID is the unique name of a message, and the others are pointers between messages.

sections.title: Quality, Language, Size and Conversion Headers
sections.content:
Quality information covers how important a message is and how it should be treated. Priority can be normal, urgent or non-urgent and can influence transmission speed and delivery. Precedence is non-standard, controversial and discouraged: it is sometimes used as a priority value that can influence transmission speed and delivery, with common values bulk and first-class, but it is also used to control automatic replies, to control return-of-content facilities and to stop mailing list loops. Importance is a hint from the originator about how important the message is, with values high, normal or low, and it is not used to control transmission speed. Sensitivity says how sensitive the message is to disclosure to people other than the specified recipients, with the values personal, private and company confidential. Incomplete-Copy says that body parts are missing.

Language information comes in two headers. Language can include a code for the natural language used in a message, for example en for English, and Content-Language does the same thing and is defined in RFC 1766. Size information includes Content-Length, which certain mailers insert to show the size in bytes of the message text as part of a format used when showing a message to its users; the memo says it should not be used when sending a message through the net, because doing so can cause several robustness and interoperability problems. Lines gives the size of the message and is a Usenet header.

Conversion control says whether the body of the message may be converted from one character set to another. Conversion has the values Prohibited and allowed, Content-Conversion is a non-standard variant with the same values, and Conversion-With-Loss says the body may not be converted if information would be lost, again with the values Prohibited and allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: These headers tell the mail system how to treat a message: how important it is, what language it is in, how big it is and whether its text may be converted into another character set.

sections.title: Encoding, Resent, Security and Miscellaneous Headers
sections.content:
Encoding information says what the content is and how it is coded. Content-Type gives the format of the content, such as the character set. Its values are defined in different ways in RFC 1049 and in MIME, so the MIME-version header is the one to look at to understand whether Content-Type is to be interpreted according to RFC 1049 or according to MIME, and the MIME definition should be used in generating mail. Content-Transfer-Encoding gives the coding method used in a MIME message body. Content-SGML-Entity carries information from the SGML entity declaration for the entity contained in the body of the body part. Encoding is used in several different ways by different mail systems, some for a kind of content-type information, some for encoding and length information, some for a kind of boundary information and some in other ways.

The resent headers exist so that when a message is forwarded by hand, the headers refer to the forwarding and not to the original message. The set is Resent-Reply-To, Resent-From, Resent-Sender, Resent-Date, Resent-To, Resent-cc, Resent-bcc and Resent-Message-ID. MIME specifies another way of resending messages, using the Message Content-Type.

Under security and reliability, Content-MD5 is a checksum of the content, so that it can be checked that the content has not been modified. Xref is a Usenet news header used to store information that stops a reader being shown the same article twice when it was sent to more than one newsgroup, and it is for local use within one Usenet news server and should not be sent between servers. The miscellaneous group includes Fcc, the name of the file in which a copy of the message is stored, Auto-Forwarded for a message that has been automatically forwarded, and the Status header, where some mail delivery systems record the delivery status when the message is stored: U for a message not downloaded and not deleted, R for read or downloaded, O for old but not deleted, D to be deleted, and N for new. Combinations such as Status: OR are used, and the memo says this header should never appear in mail in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: The last group covers how the text is encoded, what to write when you forward a message, and a checksum that says whether the body has been changed on the way.

viz.caption: THE VALUES OF THE STATUS HEADER

items.label: Not downloaded
items.desc: The message is not downloaded and not deleted.

items.label: Read
items.desc: The message is read or downloaded.

items.label: Old
items.desc: The message is old but not deleted.

items.label: To be deleted
items.desc: The message is to be deleted.

items.label: New
items.desc: The message is new; a new message is sometimes distinguished by having no Status header at all.

items.title: From
items.text: The author, or the person taking responsibility for the message.

items.title: To, cc and bcc
items.text: The primary recipients, the secondary and informational recipients, and the recipients whose names are not disclosed.

items.title: Subject
items.text: The title, often used to thread replies together.

items.title: Reply-To
items.text: Where the sender wants replies to go. The memo calls it ambiguous, because there are several kinds of reply.

items.title: Message-ID
items.text: The unique identifier of the message.
